answer_text:
Let

\[
A_3=\int_0^1 f(x)^{1/3}\,dx,\qquad
A_5=\int_0^1 f(x)^{1/5}\,dx,\qquad
A_7=\int_0^1 f(x)^{1/7}\,dx.
\]

We are given

\[
\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx=1.
\]

For any \(0<a<1\), the function \(t\mapsto t^a\) is concave on \((0,\infty)\). Hence its graph lies below its tangent line at \(t=1\):

\[
t^a \le 1+a(t-1)=a t+1-a \qquad (t>0).
\]

Apply this with \(t=f(x)\). Then

\[
f(x)^a \le a f(x)+1-a.
\]

Integrating over \([0,1]\),

\[
\int_0^1 f(x)^a\,dx
\le a\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx+\int_0^1(1-a)\,dx.
\]

Using \(\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx=1\),

\[
\int_0^1 f(x)^a\,dx \le a\cdot 1+(1-a)=1.
\]

Therefore,

\[
A_3\le 1,\qquad A_5\le 1,\qquad A_7\le 1.
\]

Since all three factors are positive,

\[
A_3A_5A_7\le 1.
\]

Equality occurs when \(f(x)=1\) for all \(x\in[0,1]\), which is allowed because \(f\) is continuous, positive, and

\[
\int_0^1 1\,dx=1.
\]

For \(f(x)\equiv 1\),

\[
A_3=A_5=A_7=1,
\]

so the product is \(1\).

Thus the maximum possible value is

\[
\boxed{1}.
\]
